title: Why You're Likely Selling to the Wrong Audience
overview: This session gave you the marketing lesson Vishen says changed everything for him: market sophistication. Through 125 years of Gillette advertising, Mindvalley's own websites and a worked leadership-coaching example, you learned the five levels a market moves through, how to tell which level yours is at, and why leading with a benefit in a crowded market is the reason many experts are not getting sales.
key_ideas: Understanding market sophistication is what let Vishen create the very first masterclass webinar in 2008, for a product called Quantum Jumping. That one masterclass did a million dollars in a month, because he finally understood he had been selling to the wrong audience - or more precisely, at the wrong level.

Dollar Shave Club turned a simple idea (razors by mail, cheaper than Gillette) into a billion-dollar company with one founder-led video. When it grew too fast, could not ship on time, raised prices and investors fired the founder who was the face of the brand, the company tanked. Two lessons: deliver on your promise, and every founder needs to be the spokesperson for their product.

The five levels through Gillette: Level 1 (1903) was a new product with no competition, so the ad simply led with the benefit - 'Shave yourself' - and sold over a million razors. Level 2, once competitors copied it, stacked a second benefit: shave yourself, look good and find a mate. Level 3 introduced a mechanism, the safety razor, with ads of a baby being shaved. Level 4 kept stacking mechanisms - the Twinjector with Telly Savalas, then lubricating strips, Fusion and ProGlide, like the car cup holder everyone had to add. Level 5 is emotion and identity: the 'best a man can get' campaign never even shows a razor.

The headline rule flips with market maturity. In an early market your headline is the benefit and the mechanism is the sub-headline; in a later market you lead with the method or mechanism and the benefit becomes the sub-headline. Mindvalley's 2003 Silva site led with 'Why do some people have it all while others stumble and crawl?' and did millions; today's meditation site leads with 'Meditation was never supposed to make you calm, it was supposed to make you unshakable' and the words performance meditation engineered.

Most experts in the room are selling at Level 1 or 2 - a benefit - to an audience that already knows the benefits of coaching, meditation or leadership training. If there is a lot of competition, the competition has already educated the market, and you need to be at Level 3 or 4 answering the question: how is your coaching different?

The leadership-coaching walk-through: 'Become a confident leader' worked 20 years ago but a thousand programmes now say it. Level 2 adds a benefit: stay confident even in the midst of chaos. Level 3 names a mechanism: learn the LEAD model by McClellan. Level 4 stacks mechanisms: the LEAD model enhanced with scenario simulations, personalised feedback and guided rehearsal. Level 5 (Great leaders think differently, like Apple's Think Different) is for big companies and most experts can skip it.

Your phraseology is how you move up in a competitive market. The Code of the Extraordinary Mind was not '10 mindset tips for a better life' but question the rules, consciousness engineering and the six-phase meditation. Marisa Peer's Rapid Transformational Therapy for Abundance stood out because it is a mechanism. Lifebook's old site led with the benefit 'Design your best life'; the new one goes straight to the mechanism, an AI-driven proven system.

The exercise: write five versions of your product headline, one for each level of sophistication, then choose the level your market is actually at. Stage 1 to 2 lead with benefit, stage 3 to 4 lead with mechanism, stage 5 builds an identity association - and for most of you the honest answer is Level 3 or 4.

frameworks.name: The 5 Levels of Market Sophistication
steps: Level 1: a new product with little competition. Lead with the single benefit (Gillette 1903: 'Shave yourself').
Level 2: competition arrives saying the same thing. Stack on a second benefit (shave yourself and look good).
Level 3: everyone has the benefit. Introduce a mechanism - a unique process or technology (the safety razor, the LEAD model).
Level 4: competitors copy the mechanism. Stack more mechanisms and up the technology (Twinjector, Fusion, ProGlide; LEAD plus simulations, feedback and rehearsal).

Level 5: mechanisms stop making sense to buyers. Big businesses shift to emotion and identity association (Gillette's 'best a man can get', Apple's Think Different). Most experts do not need this level.

frameworks.name: How the headline flips with market maturity
steps: Early market (Levels 1 to 2): headline is the benefit, sub-headline is the mechanism.
Later market (Levels 3 to 4): headline is the method or mechanism, sub-headline is the benefit.
Level 5: establish an identity association for your customer.

quotes.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
quotes.text: You must know the sophistication level of your audience before you write a single word of your copy, or your email, or your blog post, or your positioning statement.

quotes.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
quotes.text: In an early market, your headline starts with the benefit, and the mechanism is the sub-headline. In a later market, you lead with the method or the mechanism. The benefit is the sub-headline.

quotes.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
quotes.text: You must ask yourself honestly, how much competition is there? And if there's a lot of competition, the competition has educated the market.

quotes.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
quotes.text: Don't bring in benefit into a battle. It's like taking a knife to a gunfight.

quotes.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
quotes.text: You must know your mechanism, your phraseology for that mechanism, your system, your process, and that's when you start standing out.

exercises: Take a picture of the five-levels slide, then look at your own product and write down five versions of it - one headline for each level of market sophistication. You can skip Level 5 unless you are in a very competitive field such as a medical or health solution.
Ask yourself honestly how much competition you have. If there is a lot, the market is already educated, and your version should lead with the mechanism (Level 3 or 4), not the benefit.
next_steps: Write the five headline versions for your main offer this week and identify which level your market is really at.
Rewrite your current headline and sub-headline in the right order for that level: benefit first if you are early, mechanism first if the market is crowded.
Name your mechanism - the method, process or system behind your work - so you have something to lead with at Level 3 or 4.
Check the last email or post you sent: if it only promised a benefit your audience already knows, redraft it around how your approach is different.
